column4: Moses sees the fire by the mountain and hopes to find هُدًى at it, uniting the raised waymark and guidance that the section contrasts with the journey ending in a sealed fire.
The arriving crowd is مُقْتَحِمٌ and will enter the Fire; its plunge into punishment reverses the unattempted اقتحام of the life-giving pass.
The sarcastic فَمَا أَصْبَرَهُمْ عَلَى النَّارِ makes “patience” an audacity toward Fire, precisely the section’s reversal of the patience that restrains a climber on the pass.
Failure to urge طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ is given as a cause of the chained left-hand recipient’s punishment, gathering the needy person, withheld food, and the doomed side in one scene.
هَلَكَ عَنِّي سُلْطَانِيَهْ is the condemned man’s discovery that his power has vanished, answering the section’s boast of expended wealth and imagined invulnerability.
The expiation for bound oaths joins إِطْعَامُ عَشَرَةِ مَسَاكِينَ with تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ, putting the section’s oath, feeding, needy people, and opened neck in one ruling.

The ostentatious spender seeks رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ, then rain strips soil from rock and leaves the spenders unable—لَا يَقْدِرُونَ—to retain any gain; this is the section’s meeting of watched wealth, earth, and failed power.
وَالَّذِي قَدَّرَ فَهَدَى places measuring and guidance in one sequence; 87:2 supplies the preceding creation and fitting that complete the order recalled in the section.
God أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ and secured them from fear, giving the section its direct Quranic scene of a city’s people fed through hunger.
The man could have been raised by the signs but أَخْلَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ; 7:175 identifies those signs, so ascent and clinging to earth face one another exactly as in the section.
The sleepers are turned right and left while their dog stretches its forelegs بِالْوَصِيدِ, joining the two sides to the threshold word related to the section’s closing root.
إِنَّهَا عَلَيْهِم مُّؤْصَدَةٌ repeats the image of fire closed over its people and therefore supplies the closest external instance of the surah’s final closure.
أَلَمْ يَعْلَم بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَرَى answers the section’s human presumption that no one sees him, especially when he spends to be seen by people.
Those who spend their wealth رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ enact the exact contradiction developed in the section: human eyes are courted while faith in God and the Last Day is absent.
The book is placed in the man’s left hand—بِشِمَالِهِ—establishing the left-side figure whose wealth, neck, and refusal to feed the poor the section brings together.
خُذُوهُ فَغُلُّوهُ orders that the left-hand man be seized and shackled, turning the neck that was not freed into the site of restraint.
The man is inserted into a seventy-cubit chain; together with the shackle in 69:30, this supplies the bound body opposite the section’s act of opening a neck.
مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ makes the man confess that his wealth did not avail him, the direct outcome of trusting a piled and expended fortune.
Receiving the book بِیَمِینِهِ supplies the successful right-hand counterpart to the left-hand figure whose punishment and neglected poor person the section follows.
The denier is identified as the one who drives away الْيَتِيمَ, beginning a compact scene that joins the orphan to withheld food and show in worship.
He does not urge طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ; 107:2 supplies the rejected orphan and 107:6 the display before human eyes, reproducing several of the section’s meetings.
الَّذِينَ هُمْ يُرَاءُونَ adds ostentatious display to the same passage that rejects the orphan and refuses to urge feeding the needy.
The show-offs withhold even الْمَاعُونَ, making refusal of small material aid the last act in the orphan-and-hunger sequence of 107:2–6.
لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ exposes failure toward the orphan as the correction to a wealth-based account of honor and humiliation.
وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ joins the unfed needy person to the neglected orphan in 89:17 and the devoured wealth in 89:19–20.
وَتَأْكُلُونَ التُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَّمًّا makes heaped consumption of inherited property the material setting for the adjacent neglect of orphan and poor.
وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا names excessive love of wealth immediately after the orphan, poor person, and amassed inheritance, closely matching the section’s clustered images.
They feed food despite loving it to مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا, placing the needy person, orphan, and bound captive together in the positive act required by the pass.
The people of Saqar confess لَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ; 74:39 places the people of the right nearby and 74:42 asks what led the guilty into the fire.

The believers are رُحَمَاءُ بَيْنَهُمْ and are likened to a crop whose shoots support and thicken one another, directly joining mutual mercy to the section’s image of people growing together like plants.
What people withhold from God’s bounty سَيُطَوَّقُونَ around their necks on Judgment Day, turning unspent wealth into the very neck-bond that generosity should undo.
Masters are told to contract emancipation for those seeking it and give them مِن مَّالِ اللَّهِ, joining release from bondage to the transfer of wealth.
Obligatory alms are assigned both to the poor and needy and فِي الرِّقَابِ, making spent wealth serve the section’s feeding and neck-release together.
A family driven to the city by distress arrives with poor goods and asks Joseph to give full measure and charity, joining famine migration, measured provision, and merciful giving.
The city’s residents prefer migrants over themselves وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ, showing the section’s communal mercy as giving under one’s own scarcity.
فَأَمَّا مَنْ أَعْطَىٰ وَاتَّقَىٰ begins the giving branch of a paired road; 92:7 makes its destination ease, while 92:8–11 give the withholding branch.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ promises ease to the giver, illuminating the section’s difficult ascent as a moral road that God makes traversable.
The opposing traveler بَخِلَ وَاسْتَغْنَىٰ—hoards and imagines self-sufficiency—before being eased toward hardship and losing the benefit of wealth.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ is the withholding branch’s road to hardship, a reversal of both the pass’s saving difficulty and the giver’s ease in 92:7.
وَمَا يُغْنِي عَنْهُ مَالُهُ إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰ joins useless wealth to a downward fall, reversing the section’s upward leap through giving.
Humanity is addressed as toiling كَدْحًا toward its Lord and meeting Him; 84:7–12 divide that arduous journey into a right-hand reception and a fiery contrary end.
The book given بِیَمِینِهِ begins the easy reckoning branch of the same toil, directly paralleling the section’s people of the right.
The contrary recipient takes his book behind his back, a variant of the left-hand judgment scene that leads to the blaze in 84:12.
وَيَصْلَىٰ سَعِيرًا completes the adverse side of the human journey begun in 84:6 and set against the right-hand recipient in 84:7.
سَأُرْهِقُهُ صَعُودًا makes an arduous ascent a punishment for the wealthy man who resists the signs, reversing the saving ascent of the pass.
إِنَّهُ كَانَ لِآيَاتِنَا عَنِيدًا gives denial of the signs as the reason for the punitive ascent in 74:17, matching the section’s rejected signs and fiery end.
الَّذِي جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ portrays accumulated, repeatedly counted wealth in the same passage that ends with fire closed over its people in 104:8.
يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ states the wealth-holder’s delusion of immunity, corresponding to the section’s man who imagines no one can master or even see him.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God’s way are promised punishment; 9:35 turns the hoard into heated metal against their bodies.
Hoarded treasure is heated in Hell and used to brand its owners, making unspent wealth meet bodily fire in one concrete reversal.
مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ وَمَا كَسَبَ denies that wealth and earnings avail, and 111:3 immediately gives the fiery destination.
سَيَصْلَىٰ نَارًا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ makes fire the end of the wealth that could not avail in 111:2, condensing the section’s movement from piled property to fire.
When the garden’s fruit is destroyed, its owner turns his hands over what he spent while its trellises collapse, a concrete scene of trusted expenditure becoming loss.
After his garden falls, no company can help him besides God and he cannot defend himself, answering the boast that no one can overpower the wealthy man.
Against the bare rock of 2:264, sincere spending is a garden بِرَبْوَةٍ on high ground whose rain doubles its yield; height, rain, earth, and spending now produce lasting fruit.
A secure, tranquil town with abundant provision denies God’s favors and is made to taste hunger and fear, reversing the city fed from hunger and secured from fear.
فَاهْدُوهُمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطِ الْجَحِيمِ commands that wrongdoers be “guided” to the road of Hell, the sharpest reversal of a waymark that should lead the traveler safely.
The wrongdoers are granted no guiding road except طَرِيقَ جَهَنَّمَ, turning guidance and path into arrival at the fire rather than escape from it.
بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ makes the garden owners themselves deprived after they swore to deprive the poor person in 68:17 and 68:24.
اثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ and preference for the nearer life enact the downward attachment that the section places opposite being raised by the signs.
أَن تُقَطِّعُوا أَرْحَامَكُمْ makes severing womb-ties the social reversal of acting as though others emerged from the same womb and extending mercy to them.

Moses sees a fire and goes to it for news or a burning brand, repeating the night traveler’s use of distant fire for orientation and benefit, though this telling does not call the fire itself guidance.
At the side of the Mount Moses sees a fire and seeks news or a brand for his family, again joining elevation, travel, and visible fire without the explicit هُدًى wording of 20:10.
God makes fire a تَذْكِرَةً and a benefit for travelers or desert users, supporting the section’s older wayfinding-and-provision sense of fire rather than its sealed punitive sense.
The accidental-killing ruling repeatedly requires تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ, a direct Quranic occurrence of freeing a neck, though its legal occasion differs from the section’s hunger and oath scenes.
The expiation for ẓihār requires تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ before the couple touch, another concrete act of opening bondage in a different expiatory setting.
After bonds are secured in battle, captives may be released by favor or ransom; the scene gives a nonlexical instance of undoing a human bond, though it is not expressed as freeing a neck.
God has prescribed تَحِلَّةَ أَيْمَانِكُمْ, explicitly giving an oath a lawful dissolution and thus supporting the section’s movement from a tied oath to release.
The command not to break oaths بَعْدَ تَوْكِيدِهَا treats the sworn bond as something made firm, supplying the binding side of the section’s oath-and-release image.
The woman who untwists firmly spun yarn becomes the likeness for making oaths deceptive, giving the oath’s undoing a physical unbinding image after 16:91.
The garden owners أَقْسَمُوا to harvest at morning, beginning the oath that will be used to exclude the poor rather than open toward them.
وَلَا يَسْتَثْنُونَ shows the owners making no exception as they bind themselves to the harvest plan; 68:24 states its exclusion of the poor.
أَن لَّا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا الْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكُم مِّسْكِينٌ states the oath’s intended result: no poor person is to enter the garden, reversing an oath that opens into feeding.
They set out عَلَىٰ حَرْدٍ قَادِرِينَ, imagining themselves capable of enforcing deprivation; 68:27 exposes their own loss, echoing the section’s failed claim to power.
The man is given God’s signs but slips out of them; 7:176 then explains that those very signs could have raised him before he clung to the earth.
الَّذِي خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ supplies creation and fitting immediately before measuring and guidance in 87:3, completing the sequence the section sets beside the road.
Abraham asks that the city be secure and that its believing people be provided with fruits, a prayer that joins city, safety, and food like the section’s famine meeting.
Abraham places his offspring in an uncultivated valley at the Sacred House and asks for hearts to incline to them and fruits to provide for them, joining city origins, kin, and food under scarcity.
The secure sanctuary to which fruits are gathered presents the city as a protected place of provision, a close parallel to the section’s fed and secured city.
The answer about spending names relatives, orphans, needy people, and the traveler together, concretely joining wealth with the orphan’s kinship and the poor mouth.
When relatives, orphans, and needy people attend an estate division, the heirs must provide for them from it and speak kindly, making inherited wealth answer kinship and hunger.

Spending wealth is likened to a grain that grows seven ears, joining generosity to multiplication through plant growth; it supports the section’s final picture of merciful givers becoming a joined growth.
Human beings spread from one soul and its mate, and the verse invokes الْأَرْحَامَ together with God’s watchfulness, grounding the section’s “as from one womb” account of mutual mercy.
إِلَّا أَصْحَابَ الْيَمِينِ identifies the right-side group who question the guilty; 74:44 supplies the guilty people’s failure to feed the needy.
مَا سَلَكَكُمْ فِي سَقَرَ asks what inserted the guilty into Saqar, and their answer in 74:44 names failure to feed the needy; the row supplies the entry-into-fire hinge.
أَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ names the right-side company in a threefold division; 56:9 and 56:41 supply its left-side counterpart.
أَصْحَابُ الْمَشْأَمَةِ gives the left-side company opposite 56:8, repeating the two-sided classification that frames the section’s end.
The companions of the left are named again as their punishment begins; 56:42 supplies the scorching air and boiling water of that adverse destination.
فِي سَمُومٍ وَحَمِيمٍ gives the left-side company a burning environment, linking the adverse side to fiery punishment though it is not the section’s closed fire.
ثُمَّ الْجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ places the shackled man in the blaze between the neck-bond of 69:30 and the chain of 69:32.
The chained man did not believe in God the Magnificent; with 69:34, unbelief and refusing to urge food become the paired reasons for his left-side punishment.
فِي عَمَدٍ مُّمَدَّدَةٍ adds extended columns to the closure of 104:8, specifying how the fire remains shut over its people.
God says He extended ample wealth to the man who then opposed the signs and was burdened with ascent, bringing wealth into the punitive-climb scene of 74:16–17.
